item.title: Osinbajo, CJN, AGF to storm Abia for NBA-SPIDEL conference
item.description: Over 2,000 delegates expected as Otti hosts legal luminaries By Steve Oko Former Vice-President Yemi Osinbajo; the Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN), Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun; and the Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF), Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, are expected to storm Abia State for the 2026 Nigerian Bar Association Section on Public Interest and Development Law (NBA-SPIDEL) Annual Conference. The conference, scheduled for November 9–13 at the International Conference Centre, Umuahia, is expected to attract over 2,000 participants, including judges, lawyers, policymakers, civil society organisations, academics and development partners. The Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Sir Ikechukwu Uwanna, disclosed this during a press conference at the Ministry of Justice, Umuahia, assuring participants of the state government’s commitment to a successful hosting. Uwanna said Governor Alex Otti would declare the conference open, adding that the gathering would offer participants an opportunity to assess firsthand the transformation taking place in Abia’s justice and correctional sectors. He urged NBA-SPIDEL to ensure that the conference produced practical recommendations capable of strengthening the justice system and improving citizens’ welfare, rather than ending with mere intellectual discussions. The Solicitor-General and Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Justice, Sir Paul Ogubunka, and NBA-SPIDEL Chairperson, Prof. Uju Agomoh, said the conference would provide a platform for legal practitioners and other stakeholders to promote justice, strengthen democratic institutions, protect fundamental rights and advance development through the rule of law. They noted that the gathering would facilitate critical discussions on justice delivery, democratic governance and institutional development. The Chairman of the Central Planning Committee, Sir Ejike Ezenwa, SAN; the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor on Legal Matters, Mrs Nkolika Ubani; and the Media and Publicity Subcommittee Chairman, Mr Obiefule Chikezie, said the conference would feature pre-conference engagements, professional development sessions and technical sessions. They commended the Otti administration for its strides in the justice sector and expressed optimism that the conference would further strengthen justice delivery and the rule of law in the state. item.title: The Signal: INEC Draws The Line, The Politicians Must Now Face The Voters
item.description: An important decision on governorship candidates, fresh pressure over the voters’ register, and a new battle for the South-East have shifted the 2027 campaign into more consequential territory. The politicians are still negotiating power. The electoral commission is beginning to determine who can contest it. For weeks, Nigeria’s political conversation has revolved around familiar questions. Who is supporting President Bola Tinubu? Can Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi agree on a common strategy? How much influence does Nyesom Wike command? Which governor will deliver which state? Then, on Friday, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) reminded everyone that there is another player in this election: the umpire. INEC announced the outcome of its review of complaints arising from the exclusion of governorship and state assembly candidates. Some politicians received welcome news. Others discovered that their appeals had failed. Among the most notable decisions, former Communications Minister Isa Pantami succeeded in his petition concerning the Gombe governorship election, although his candidacy remains subject to pending litigation. Ladi Adebutu, the PDP’s governorship candidate in Ogun State, was less fortunate. His petition was rejected. These decisions may appear to be administrative matters. They are not. They affect the choices available to voters, the calculations of political parties, and potentially the balance of power in important states. And they arrive at a moment when INEC is already facing intense scrutiny over the integrity of the voters’ register. The emerging question is no longer simply which politician has the strongest campaign organisation. It is whether Nigeria’s electoral institutions can apply the rules consistently, resolve disputes transparently and command public confidence when the votes are counted. Pantami gets a reprieve. Adebutu does not. INEC’s latest decisions offer a revealing picture of the difficulties political parties are experiencing with the Electoral Act and candidate nomination procedures. The commission received 69 petitions from 12 political parties across 26 states concerning governorship nominations. Of those, 41 succeeded, and 28 were rejected. For state assembly elections, 25 of the 61 petitions were successful, while 36 were rejected. The figures tell us something important. This is not an isolated disagreement involving one or two politicians. It is a substantial problem affecting party nominations across the country. The disputes concern membership registers, compliance with statutory deadlines, alleged multiple nominations and the wrongful inclusion or exclusion of candidates. INEC says it examined the complaints against relevant records and legal provisions. In Gombe, Pantami’s successful petition offers the PDP an opportunity to compete with a candidate whose exclusion had threatened its position in the state. But the pending court proceedings mean that the matter is not entirely settled

This is not an isolated disagreement involving one or two politicians. It is a substantial problem affecting party nominations across the country. The disputes concern membership registers, compliance with statutory deadlines, alleged multiple nominations and the wrongful inclusion or exclusion of candidates. INEC says it examined the complaints against relevant records and legal provisions. In Gombe, Pantami’s successful petition offers the PDP an opportunity to compete with a candidate whose exclusion had threatened its position in the state. But the pending court proceedings mean that the matter is not entirely settled. In Ogun, Adebutu’s unsuccessful appeal presents a different challenge. Unless the decision is overturned through a lawful process, the PDP faces the prospect of contesting the wider election without its preferred governorship candidate on the ballot. That could have consequences beyond the governorship race. State-level campaigns help mobilise supporters for other elections. They provide organisational networks, local leadership and political visibility. A party without a governorship candidate may find it more difficult to sustain enthusiasm among its supporters. But there is also a larger principle. Political parties cannot demand strict compliance with electoral law from INEC while treating their own statutory obligations as optional. If the law requires membership registers to be submitted within a prescribed period, parties must comply. Equally, INEC must demonstrate that it applies those requirements fairly to every party, whether ruling or opposition. The commission’s willingness to uphold some petitions and reject others is evidence of a review process. It is not, by itself, proof that every decision was correct. That judgment must rest on the law, the records and, where necessary, the courts. The lesson is simple: an election can be lost before polling day if a political party fails to get its nominations right. The Register Controversy Takes A More Troubling Turn If the candidate-list decisions were the day’s most consequential administrative development, the controversy surrounding the voters’ register may prove even more serious. On Friday, INEC’s Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, acknowledged that some registration officers had introduced irregular records into the commission’s database. Among the questionable entries were photographs suspected or identified as artificially generated, alongside other defective registration records. Bayode said the commission had identified how some irregularities entered the system, although the motives of those responsible remained unclear. This changes the nature of the discussion. Until now, much of the controversy had centred on screenshots circulating online and allegations from political actors. INEC’s acknowledgment provides a firmer basis for examining weaknesses in the registration process. But two distinctions are essential. First, the register under examination is preliminary, not final. INEC says its verification and cleanup processes are continuing ahead of certification on December 15. Second, the discovery of irregular entries does not establish that fraudulent votes have been cast, or that the irregularities were introduced to benefit any particular candidate. Those distinctions must not be lost in the political argument. Nevertheless, serious questions arise. How many questionable records have been identified? Were registration officers able to circumvent existing safeguards? How many records have been removed? What disciplinary or criminal investigations are underway? And perhaps most importantly, how will INEC demonstrate that its final register has been properly verified? Atiku Abubakar has demanded an independent forensic audit, identification of the officers involved, and disclosure of contractors handling sensitive election materials. He has also threatened legal action if the commission fails to provide the information sought. These demands are part of the opposition’s political response, but the underlying issue extends beyond party competition. Every candidate has an interest in an accurate register. So does every voter. INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan declared on Friday, during a meeting with an ECOWAS pre-election delegation, that the commission has no preferred candidate or political party. He said INEC had completed nine of the 14 major milestones in its election timetable and outlined preparations involving biometric accreditation and electronic results management. Those assurances are important. But they must be accompanied by evidence of corrective action. The danger is not simply that irregular records may remain in the database. It is that uncertainty about the register could undermine public acceptance of the eventual election result. INEC has an opportunity to prevent that outcome. It should use it. item.title: ‘I cry, break down behind closed doors’ – Funke Akindele reflects on pressures of being in the spotlight
item.description: By Aiyedun Oluwadamilola Nollywood actress and producer Funke Akindele has opened up about her emotional struggles behind the cameras, revealing that she sometimes cries and breaks down in private despite her cheerful public image. The actress made this known during an interview with CNN, where she reflected on the pressures of fame, public scrutiny of her relationships and the importance of prioritising personal well-being. “I cry. I lock myself in the room, cry, break down, and hit the bed. But I just pick myself up and come back to life,” Akindele said. The filmmaker, popularly associated with her ability to entertain audiences through her films and public appearances, acknowledged that the cheerful image people see does not always reflect what she experiences privately. She also spoke about the effect of public opinion on her personal life, recalling moments when she questioned her decisions and worried about how people would judge her. “Sometimes I tell myself, you’ve made a mistake again. How are people going to judge you?” she said, describing the thoughts she sometimes had to overcome. Akindele explained that she has gradually learnt to confront challenges and move forward rather than allow public opinion to determine how she sees herself. Beyond dealing with criticism, the actress highlighted the importance of self-care and maintaining relationships with loved ones while pursuing professional success. We therefore appeal to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, whose leadership we support and will continue to support, to look closely at the men behind this scheme,” they said. Describing Uzodimma as the heartbeat of the APC in the South-East, the chairmen said they remained loyal party members but urged the APC to move quickly to resolve what they called a “robbery” before it causes problems for the party in the region. “While we hope and pray that this sinister action of enemies of Ndigbo will be quashed by the Appeal Court, we fear the backlash of this obnoxious attempt to deny the people of the South East their rightful political position of being at least the number three in Nigeria, something that has been denied us for almost 20 years,” they said. The judgment, in suit number FHC/ABJ/CS/1854/2026, ended a case Okorocha filed on August 13 against INEC, the APC and Uzodimma. Primaries records At the heart of the case are conflicting records of the primary. Okorocha’s affidavit, filed by his son, Amen Rochas, claimed he polled 150,780 votes to Uzodimma’s 102,158. Its Publicity Secretary, Onwuasoanya FCC Jones, said in a statement that Uzodimma “remains the candidate of our party for Imo West Senatorial District.” He said the party’s legal department would study the ruling and act accordingly. The Uzodimma camp has said he will appeal. Okorocha, through his Chief Press Secretary, Sam Onwuemeodo, called the judgment “a victory for the nation’s fast-growing democracy.” He thanked President Tinubu and the APC leadership for creating an environment in which members could pursue their rights. He said talk of his arrest had been put to rest, “because the court has found that my documents are genuine and correct.” Okorocha said INEC does not conduct party primaries but only monitors them and holds whatever the party deposits. According to him, the results transmitted to INEC headquarters were in his favour, but a different result was announced after the party told states not to announce results. He said he obtained certified copies of the primary documents from INEC on July 22, 2026, while the governor’s document emerged a month later, on August 22, which he called “an afterthought.” He said the irregularities in the governor’s documents were what the court looked at. In his account, the document puts the primary on May 16, two days before the actual date, and describes the governor as a consensus candidate in what was a direct primary. Uzodimma’s side has not responded to these claims. Uzodimma’s lawyers had argued that a litigant seeking to be declared winner of a primary must file within 14 days, yet Okorocha filed 87 days after. Okorocha rejected this, saying he held a certified true copy from INEC showing he won. “I can’t sue myself as a winner,” he said. The contest also carries a complication unrelated to the ballot box. Uzodimma was first sworn in as governor on January 15, 2020, and re-elected in November 2023, and his term runs until January 2028. He will therefore still be governor when the Senate election holds. item.description: By Muhammad Inuwa, Dutse ‎ ‎A chieftain of the All Progressives Congress, APC, and former House of Representative member representing Birnin-Kudu/ Buji in Jigawa State, Engr. Magaji Da’u Aliyu, has claimed that Northern political leaders begged President Bola Tinubu to support former President Muhammadu Buhari’s presidential ambition and promised to return power to his side after eight years. ‎Aliyu, who is also the Deputy Campaign Director of the North for Tinubu Support Group, disclosed this while addressing supporters in Birnin Kudu. ‎He said the North has no justification for opposing Tinubu’s re-election in the 2027 general election, insisting that the region must honour the political agreement allegedly reached before Buhari became president in 2015. ‎ ‎According to him, Buhari had contested the presidential election three times without success before Northern political leaders approached Tinubu in Lagos to seek his support. ‎ ‎”Buhari contested the presidential election three times and lost. We then went to Lagos to beg Tinubu to support Buhari’s presidential ambition,” he said. ‎ ‎”He agreed to support us on the understanding that after Buhari’s eight years in office, power would return to his side, and we accepted the agreement.” ‎ ‎Aliyu maintained that supporting Tinubu’s re-election in 2027 is a matter of honouring the promise made to him, stressing that Northerners have no reason to abandon the agreement. ‎ ‎”For every Northerner, fulfilling that agreement is mandatory. item.title: Drunk barber allegedly stabs man to death in Jigawa
item.description: By Muhammad Inuwa, Dutse The Jigawa State Police Command has arrested a 29-year-old barber, Emmanuel Olatonok, for allegedly stabbing a 32-year-old man, Ibrahim Shago, to death while reportedly under the influence of alcohol. The Police Public Relations Officer, SP Shiisu Lawan Adam, disclosed this in a statement issued to journalists. The incident occurred on Thursday, October 29, 2026, at about 5:45 p.m. in the Rafin Sanyi area of Dutse Local Government Area. According to the police spokesperson, the suspect, who reportedly worked as a barber at a hotel in Dutse, allegedly stabbed the victim in the neck with a knife following an argument. He added that the suspect was allegedly under the influence of alcohol at the time of the incident. “The suspect, a barber reportedly working at a popular hotel in Dutse, allegedly stabbed the victim in the neck with a knife following an argument,” he said. Adam explained that the victim, a resident of Karnaya town, was immediately rushed to a hospital for medical attention but was later confirmed dead by a medical doctor. He said the incident triggered tension in the area as some angry youths gathered at the scene and attempted to vandalise the hotel. However, police operatives from Dutse Division quickly intervened and brought the situation under control, preventing further violence and destruction of property. The police spokesperson confirmed that the suspect is currently in custody, while investigations are ongoing to establish the circumstances surrounding the killing. He added that the suspect would be charged to court upon the conclusion of the investigation. item.title: 21 cars affected as fire engulfs Lagos mechanic workshop
item.description: By Evelyn Usman A mechanic workshop went up in flames in the early hours of yesterday at Isheri-Idimu, Alimosho Local Government Area of Lagos State, with 21 vehicles reportedly affected. The fire, which broke out at about 3:05am on Oladunni Street, beside Eternal Filling Station, reportedly threatened to spread to the adjoining petrol station, raising fears of a possible major disaster, according to eyewitnesses. However, the swift intervention of emergency responders reportedly prevented the inferno from spreading to the filling station and nearby buildings. The Lagos State Emergency Management Agency (LASEMA) said its Dolphin Response Team, stationed at Igando, was immediately activated following a distress call. The Permanent Secretary of LASEMA, Dr Olufemi Oke-Osanyintolu, said: “Upon arrival, responders discovered that the fire had engulfed a mechanical workshop where several exotic vehicles were parked, in close proximity to a petroleum filling station. Through the prompt, professional and coordinated intervention of the LASEMA Response Team and the Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service, supported by the Lagos Neighbourhood Safety Corps and the Nigeria Police Force, the inferno was prevented from spreading to the filling station and surrounding structures, thereby averting what could have been a major disaster. “The fire has been completely extinguished and damping-down operations concluded. Preliminary assessment indicates that about twenty-one (21) exotic vehicles were affected, with a section of a nearby building sustaining minor damage. “Importantly, no loss of life and no injury were recorded. “The Lagos State Government, through LASEMA, reiterates its commitment to the protection of lives and property across the state. The agency commends the bravery and diligence of all responders whose swift action ensured that the incident was brought under control without casualties. “Members of the public are enjoined to continue to prioritise safety measures, particularly in workshops and environments where inflammable materials are handled, and to promptly alert emergency services through the toll-free emergency numbers 767 and 112 in the event of any emergency,” he said. With Nigeria’s population estimated at approximately 220 million and a youthful demographic, Alausa argued that education reform was imperative. The challenge is to turn this demographic advantage into economic productivity rather than allow it to deepen unemployment, inequality and insecurity Perhaps the most consequential element of Alausa’s presentation was the ministry’s cloud-based education dashboard, which he said captures information on nearly 46 million children. Its potential lies in replacing fragmented administrative records with a more comprehensive picture of the education system. Reliable information could help authorities identify schools without adequate classrooms, locate teacher shortages, track enrolment and attendance, and direct resources towards underserved communities. For years, inadequate or inconsistent data have complicated education planning. Children who drop out may disappear from official records, while schools with urgent needs may struggle to attract appropriate interventions. A functioning digital system could change that by helping policymakers identify problems early and monitor whether government investments produce results.But there is a crucial distinction between collecting data and using it effectively. The minister’s presentation did not independently establish the completeness of the dashboard’s coverage, the frequency of updates or the extent to which its information has been verified against school-level records. For the system to become a credible accountability instrument, its data must be regularly updated, independently validated and linked to decisions on funding and intervention. Appropriate information should also be accessible to researchers, journalists and the public, without compromising children’s privacy. Otherwise, the dashboard risks becoming an expensive digital catalogue of problems rather than an instrument for solving them. Back to school Among the most compelling claims in Alausa’s presentation was that the government had brought approximately one million children back into school over the preceding three years. If independently verified and sustained, the achievement would represent a significant step towards addressing Nigeria’s persistent out-of-school crisis.Yet, educational exclusion is not simply a question of school admission. Poverty, insecurity, displacement, child labour, early marriage, inadequate infrastructure and the cost of schooling all contribute to keeping children away from classrooms. In conflict-affected communities, children may be enrolled but unable to attend safely. In poor households, the immediate need for income can outweigh the perceived benefits of education. Girls may face additional barriers, including household responsibilities, early marriage and inadequate sanitation facilities. Consequently, returning a child to school is only the beginning. The government must establish how many of the reported one million children remain enrolled, attend consistently, progress through school and acquire foundational literacy and numeracy skills. It must also demonstrate that interventions are reaching the hardest-to-reach populations, particularly children in remote rural settlements, economically disadvantaged households and communities affected by insecurity. Without transparent definitions, a clear baseline and independently verifiable evidence, the reported figure cannot by itself establish the extent to which Nigeria’s out-of-school crisis has been reduced. The country needs not merely children counted in school records, but children who attend, learn and complete their education. Another major pillar of Alausa’s agenda is technical and vocational education and training, under which he reported that nearly 250,000 Nigerians were undergoing skills training. The initiative challenges the longstanding perception that conventional university education is the principal route to success. The decisive questions concern the quality of instruction, relevance of the courses, availability of modern equipment and whether participants obtain recognised qualifications. The government should publish completion rates, certification figures and employment outcomes to establish whether the initiative is creating genuine pathways to economic mobility. Without such evidence, Nigeria risks producing another generation of certificate holders without the practical competencies employers need. item.title: 46-yr-old businessman commits suicide, leaves video message for family
item.description: By Dayo Johnson, Akure A 46-year-old businessman, Akinbolusere Kayode, has reportedly died by suicide in Ondo Town, Ondo State. Sources said he took his life in his office near BOVAS Petrol Station in Igba Town at about 3 p.m. on Thursday. Two empty bottles suspected to have contained poisonous substance were recovered by police detectives attached to the Bolorunduro Division who visited the scene. According to sources, the deceased recorded a video in which he spoke about his business challenges, humble beginnings, and relationship with his wife, whom he praised for standing by him throughout his struggles. He also repeatedly stated that no one pressured him into deciding to transfer his properties to his wife and three children. The state Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Jimoh Abayomi, confirmed the incident. Abayomi said the two empty bottles suspected to have contained Sniper insecticide were recovered from a nearby bush during the police investigation. He added that preliminary findings indicated that the deceased recorded a video before his death in which he lamented the hardships he faced in life. The video has since circulated widely on social media. His remains were evacuated and deposited at the State Hospital morgue for preservation and further examination. Police said no signs of foul play or visible injuries were observed on the body during the initial examination. The Commissioner of Police in the state, Felix Ohagwu, has ordered a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident to determine the actual cause of death. Ohagwu urged members of the public to refrain from speculation and allow investigators to carry out their work. He also advised individuals experiencing emotional distress, marital difficulties, or other personal challenges to seek timely support and assistance rather than resorting to actions that could endanger their lives. item.content:encoded: By Dayo Johnson, Akure A 46-year-old businessman, Akinbolusere Kayode, has reportedly died by suicide in Ondo Town, Ondo State. Sources said he took his life in his office near BOVAS Petrol Station in Igba Town at about 3 p.m. on Thursday. Two empty bottles suspected to have contained poisonous substance were recovered by police detectives attached to the Bolorunduro Division who visited the scene. According to sources, the deceased recorded a video in which he spoke about his business challenges, humble beginnings, and relationship with his wife, whom he praised for standing by him throughout his struggles. He also repeatedly stated that no one pressured him into deciding to transfer his properties to his wife and three children. The state Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Jimoh Abayomi, confirmed the incident. Abayomi said the two empty bottles suspected to have contained Sniper insecticide were recovered from a nearby bush during the police investigation. He added that preliminary findings indicated that the deceased recorded a video before his death in which he lamented the hardships he faced in life. The video has since circulated widely on social media. His remains were evacuated and deposited at the State Hospital morgue for preservation and further examination. Police said no signs of foul play or visible injuries were observed on the body during the initial examination. The Commissioner of Police in the state, Felix Ohagwu, has ordered a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident to determine the actual cause of death. Ohagwu urged members of the public to refrain from speculation and allow investigators to carry out their work. He also advised individuals experiencing emotional distress, marital difficulties, or other personal challenges to seek timely support and assistance rather than resorting to actions that could endanger their lives. Yetunde Akinola, Consultant Pharmacist and Pharmaceutical Care Specialist said, “The increasing circulation of fake and counterfeit medicines in Nigeria exposes serious weaknesses in the pharmaceutical supply chain and presents a grave danger to the health and safety of citizens. A counterfeit medicine is one that is deliberately and fraudulently misrepresented in terms of its identity, composition or source. Such products may contain incorrect ingredients, inadequate quantities of active pharmaceutical substances, no active ingredients at all or potentially harmful contaminants. There are also substandard medicines, which are authorised products that fail to meet the required quality standards. “The danger is that many of these products are packaged to look exactly like genuine medicines, making it difficult for unsuspecting members of the public to distinguish between them. item.title: Masussuka: Life, preaching, death
item.description: The murder of Katsina-based Islamic cleric, Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka, has stirred emotions and sparked conversations around the life and times of a popular preacher seen through different lenses. To his army of followers, he embodied peace, dignity and tolerance for religious differences. To his critics, he was a controversial scholar whose religious ideology and preaching were questionable. Masussuka was shot dead alongside his associate, Adamu Abubakar, on Monday evening in front of his house at Dutsin-Ma, Katsina State, in an attack claimed by the extremist group, Ansaru. Amnesty International has called on the Nigerian government to conduct a thorough investigation into the killing and ensure that those responsible are brought to justice. Masussuka: We reject his ideology but condemn his killing – JIBWIS Imam Masussuka’s preaching, killing contrary to Islamic laws – Sheikh Maraya The 47-year-old cleric subscribed to and preached Quranic teachings, but, to greater extent, disregarded Hadith, the sayings and practices of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) – a stance that placed him at variance with his critics. He alleged that a lot of Hadiths being attributed to the Prophet were not from him, saying they were concocted by some people out of mischief. Masussuka reportedly began preaching at the tender age of 13 and rose to prominence with the advent of social media, through which he established himself as one of the most vocal clerics among the Qur’aniyun Islamic sect. item.content:encoded: The murder of Katsina-based Islamic cleric, Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka, has stirred emotions and sparked conversations around the life and times of a popular preacher seen through different lenses. To his army of followers, he embodied peace, dignity and tolerance for religious differences. To his critics, he was a controversial scholar whose religious ideology and preaching were questionable. Masussuka was shot dead alongside his associate, Adamu Abubakar, on Monday evening in front of his house at Dutsin-Ma, Katsina State, in an attack claimed by the extremist group, Ansaru. Amnesty International has called on the Nigerian government to conduct a thorough investigation into the killing and ensure that those responsible are brought to justice. Masussuka: We reject his ideology but condemn his killing – JIBWIS Imam Masussuka’s preaching, killing contrary to Islamic laws – Sheikh Maraya The 47-year-old cleric subscribed to and preached Quranic teachings, but, to greater extent, disregarded Hadith, the sayings and practices of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) – a stance that placed him at variance with his critics. He alleged that a lot of Hadiths being attributed to the Prophet were not from him, saying they were concocted by some people out of mischief. Masussuka reportedly began preaching at the tender age of 13 and rose to prominence with the advent of social media, through which he established himself as one of the most vocal clerics among the Qur’aniyun Islamic sect. Through his active social media platforms, his preaching gained more recognition, increasingly attracting attention from other sects with different ideologies. Masussuka’s increased visibility drew controversies around his ideology. One major controversy surrounding Masussuka’s teachings and ideology revolved around his rejection of certain Hadith traditions as authorities and forms of religious practice. According to other sects, his doctrine that only the Qur’an serves as the gateway to religious practice goes contrary to a larger belief that both the Qur’an and the Sunnah of the Prophet are central sources of Islamic guidance. Disagreements over his ideology became more pronounced and his teachings were challenged on several occasions. Though disagreement on the interpretation and authority of Hadith has long existed among Muslim scholars, Masussuka’s unique stance on the matter placed him at odds with scholars who considered his teachings inconsistent with established Islamic traditions. Amid growing scrutiny of his preaching, the Katsina State Government, on November 18, 2025, announced that Masussuka would be required to defend his teachings before a committee of Islamic scholars established based on the several calls. The meeting, however, didn’t see the light of day due to undisclosed circumstances, as he continued to challenge other sects that go against his ideologies. Sources close to the late cleric revealed that his doctrine attracted several death threats, but he didn’t take them seriously as he restrained his followers from reacting. His killing has left many questions amid renewed concern over the safety of clerics across the northern region. Masussuka’s murder was not the first in the North. Over the years, prominent Islamic clerics like late Sheikh Umaru Dan Me Shiyya, Sheikh Jafar Mahmud Adam and Sheikh Auwal Albani Zaria were all victims of cold-blooded murder. A day after his killing, Boko Haram breakaway group, Ansaru, took responsibility for the attack in a viral audio clip. A security analyst, Dr Audu Bulama Bukarti, also linked the cleric’s killing to Ansaru, noting that the released audio had been confirmed to be from the Ansaru group. But Masussuka’s family has rejected the claim and questioned the authenticity of the audio. Childhood The late cleric was born in Yauyau village in the present-day Batsari Local Government Area to a family of pastoralists. His parents relocated to Masussuka in Ningi Local Government Area of Bauchi State when he was a toddler. He started his Qur’anic education in Masussuka village before he left for other towns and villages and returned to Katsina in search of Islamic knowledge. He attended the Arabic Teachers College in Katsina, but dropped out and went to Malam Zakariya Qur’anic School in Sabuwar Unguwa area of the state. Malam Ismail Zakariya, the son of his late teacher (Malam Zakariya) and proprietor of the school, told Weekend Trust that the cleric stayed at the school for about seven years before he relocated to Dutsin-Ma town. According to Ismail, Masussuka, besides his persistent pursuit of Islamic knowledge, was highly entrepreneurial, dealing in traditional medicines (local herbs) to sustain himself and his family. He recalled the late cleric was arrested at the height of Boko Haram in 2000, on the suspicion that he had links with some terror groups. He was later absolved of the allegation and released unconditionally. “My father, Malam Zakariya, engaged the security agency then and secured his release. The allegation prevented Masussuka from securing a house in Katsina City and he decided to leave Katsina for Dutsin-Ma,” Ismail said. Ismail stated that those who disagreed with Masussuka’s preaching do so for selfish reasons. He said, “Everyone knows the Qur’an is one scripture that cannot be altered, but what matters is the interpretation depending on how one views it and the nature of the audience. “Hadith is the only point of contention between the Qur’aniyyun sect and the Muslims from the other sects and even those who believe in Hadith have admitted that some are prescribed as weak and others as genuine and authenticated. “To me, the approach Masussuka adopted in explaining and interpreting those portions during preachings earned him more enemies than followers, but beyond that, there is nothing different from what other Muslim scholars preached,” he said. He respected me as a teacher and a father,” Adam said. According to him, many scholars who opposed Masussuka’s preaching did so “out of hatred for the truth.” According to him, “he may be wrong in his approach to presentation or interpretation as a human being, but I can tell you for free that Masussuka never compromised, saying things as they are and that could be the reason he earned more enemies. Masari, who is considered one of the influential APC figures in Katsina, was absent during the inauguration of the Dikko/Tinubu Campaign Council by Governor Dikko Umaru Radda. He was also missing at the official flag-off of the campaign in Funtua Local Government Area. However, rather than joining the governor at the public campaign events, Masari is said to have intensified separate political consultations within and outside Katsina State ahead of the 2027 general elections. His recent engagements suggest efforts to build support for the Tinubu-Radda re-election project through religious leaders, academics, former political office holders, grassroots organisations, party stakeholders, community influencers and members of the business community. On October 26, Masari held a meeting with 1,121 Islamic clerics in Katsina, comprising members of the Qadiriyya and Tijjaniyya orders, the Izala movement, as well as male, female and youth Islamic scholars. At the meeting, he reportedly appealed to the religious leaders to communicate their positions to their congregations and encourage eligible voters to support President Tinubu. Similarly, on October 9, Masari was among prominent Katsina political figures who attended a high-level APC stakeholders’ meeting convened by Governor Radda at the Katsina State Governor’s Lodge in Abuja. Although details of the discussions were not made public, the meeting was held behind closed doors amid preparations by the ruling party for the 2027 elections. Earlier, on October 2, Masari inaugurated two political support organisations in Katsina: the Wazirin Tinubu Ambassador Movement and the 360Plus1 Support. The initiatives were reportedly designed to strengthen grassroots mobilisation for the Tinubu-Radda ticket. He also received the leadership of the Joint Islamic First Aid Organisation in Abuja during the same month. The delegation was led by its chairman, Ahmad Jingi Adamu. Masari had also engaged senior academics from universities across the country in September 2026 during a high-level meeting themed, “Consolidating the Renewed Hope Agenda: Three Years of President Tinubu’s Achievements and the Road to 2027.” In another political engagement, he addressed thousands of APC supporters and political stakeholders at Nabanje, his hometown in Kafur Local Government Area, as part of efforts to consolidate support for the ruling party. The ICC Director-General, Abubakar Abdullahi-Matazu, disclosed that the council had established a five-member structure for each polling unit across the state to strengthen its grassroots presence ahead of the elections. According to him, it is only then that the underlying disagreements, political rivalries and other issues within the party may fully emerge into the public domain. “With all the visible indicators showing the existing rift between the two Katsina APC big wigs and taking into consideration the INEC’s elections timetable, it will be very difficult to see the real misunderstanding indices between the two, but believe me, whatsoever is the issue, it will be visible after the presidential election,” he said. Our correspondent reports that despite repeated reconciliation efforts over the past three years, including another reported peace initiative in less than a week, the political differences between the two leaders remain unresolved, with the Akume-aligned faction insisting that support for Tinubu does not automatically translate into support for Alia, while the governor’s camp maintains that it is focused on governance rather than rival political alliances. From industrial-scale drug production to cocaine couriers and cross-border syndicates, the persistence of the illicit trade raises questions about the sophistication of criminal networks and the factors sustaining the business. The growing drug problem has continued to impact negatively on the health and general wellbeing of many Nigerians, especially the youth population. Many families and households note that they are going through a lot of trauma and pains in the management and rehabilitation of their children and loved ones who have become victims of drug addiction. Today, he struggles to come to terms with the consequences of his past, particularly when he compares his life with those of friends and younger siblings who have moved ahead of him. “Drug abuse affected me significantly in ways I regret today. I can’t even measure up or stand where my friends are now. I feel inferior. “In terms of education, I am way behind, as even my younger siblings, both male and female, are far ahead of me. “However, I thank God that I am now okay and coming back to my senses, although I still take some of these intoxicants to calm myself sometimes,” he said For his mother, Raihanatu Musa, watching her son struggle with drug addiction was one of the most painful experiences of her life. She described the ordeal as a test of faith, recalling how the situation almost tore the family apart in her determination not to abandon him to his fate. “It was a real test from God. item.title: Debt Worse Than Leprosy, Destroys Generations, Says Obasanjo
item.description: Former President Olusegun Obasanjo has criticised President Bola Tinubu over his position on borrowing, declaring that debt is worse than leprosy because it destroys generations. He stated this while speaking at a symposium, a public forum focused on leveraging Artificial Intelligence to solve grassroots problems and accelerate national development in Abeokuta, Ogun State. Tinubu had said in April that borrowing should not be viewed negatively, insisting that the government would borrow when necessary, provided it could repay the loans. item.title: Fani-Kayode Presents Letters Of Credence, Assumes Duties As High Commissioner In South Africa
item.description: A former Minister of Aviation, Femi Fani-Kayode, has formally presented copies of his Letters of Credence to the Deputy Director-General, Public Diplomacy, and Acting Chief of State Protocol, Mr Clayson Monyela, at the South African Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO). The presentation on Friday marked an important diplomatic milestone, signifying the formal commencement of Fani-Kayode’s diplomatic functions and his assumption of duties as Nigeria’s High Commissioner to South Africa with effect from October 30, 2026. This photo shows Nigeria’s High Commissioner to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode (centre), meeting with South African officials on October 30, 2026. Following the presentation, Fani-Kayode also met with the Deputy Director-General of DIRCO in his office, as part of his initial diplomatic engagements with senior South African government officials. The presentation of copies of his Letters of Credence precedes the ceremonial presentation of his Letters of Credence to South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa, which will take place in a few days. This photo shows Nigeria’s High Commissioner to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode (left), presenting his Letters of Credence on October 30, 2026. In a statement dated October 28, the Department of International Relations and Cooperation of the Republic of South Africa explained that the Minister of International Relations and Cooperation had approved a policy change in terms of Article 13 (1) of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961, to replace the current practice where a Head of Mission-Designate would have to present the original Letters of Credence to the President before being considered as having taken up their functions in the receiving state. “The Department wishes to confirm that once the Head of Mission-Designate has submitted the copies of the Letters of Credence to the Chief of State Protocol, the said Head of Mission-Designate is considered to have taken up his / her position as Head of Mission,” the statement read in part. “The Department wishes to furthermore confirm that the original Letters of Credence will still be handed over to the President at the next Credentials Ceremony on a date and time to be communicated. The Department of International Relations and Cooperation of the Republic of South Africa avails itself of this opportunity to renew to the High Commission of the Federal Republic of Nigeria the assurances of its highest consideration.” The post Fani-Kayode Presents Letters Of Credence, Assumes Duties As High Commissioner In South Africa appeared first on Channels Television .
